claim: To date there exists no reliable method to non-invasively upregulate or downregulate the state of the resting human motor system over a large dynamic range.
source: To date there exists no reliable method to non-invasively upregulate or downregulate the state of the resting human motor system over a large dynamic range.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field presented in the abstract without specific supporting data or citations in this sentence.

claim: An operant conditioning paradigm which provides neurofeedback of the size of motor evoked potentials (MEPs) in response to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), enables participants to self-modulate their own brain state.
source: Here we show that an operant conditioning paradigm which provides neurofeedback of the size of motor evoked potentials (MEPs) in response to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), enables participants to self-modulate their own brain state.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Following training, participants were able to robustly increase MEP amplitudes by 83.8%.
source: Following training, participants were able to robustly increase (by 83.8%) and decrease (by 30.6%) their MEP amplitudes.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Following training, participants were able to robustly decrease MEP amplitudes by 30.6%.
source: Following training, participants were able to robustly increase (by 83.8%) and decrease (by 30.6%) their MEP amplitudes.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data.

claim: Volitional up-versus down-regulation of corticomotor excitability caused an increase of late-cortical disinhibition (LCD).
source: This volitional up-versus down-regulation of corticomotor excitability caused an increase of late-cortical disinhibition (LCD), a TMS derived read-out of presynaptic GABAB disinhibition, which was accompanied by an increase of gamma and a decrease of alpha oscillations in the trained hemisphere.
evidence: This claim is supported by paired-pulse TMS measurements presented in the results.

claim: Late-cortical disinhibition (LCD) is a TMS derived read-out of presynaptic GABAB disinhibition.
source: This volitional up-versus down-regulation of corticomotor excitability caused an increase of late-cortical disinhibition (LCD), a TMS derived read-out of presynaptic GABAB disinhibition, which was accompanied by an increase of gamma and a decrease of alpha oscillations in the trained hemisphere.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about LCD and is also cited in the discussion section.

claim: Volitional up-regulation of corticomotor excitability was accompanied by an increase of gamma oscillations in the trained hemisphere.
source: This volitional up-versus down-regulation of corticomotor excitability caused an increase of late-cortical disinhibition (LCD), a TMS derived read-out of presynaptic GABAB disinhibition, which was accompanied by an increase of gamma and a decrease of alpha oscillations in the trained hemisphere.
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG data presented in the results.

claim: Volitional up-regulation of corticomotor excitability was accompanied by a decrease of alpha oscillations in the trained hemisphere.
source: This volitional up-versus down-regulation of corticomotor excitability caused an increase of late-cortical disinhibition (LCD), a TMS derived read-out of presynaptic GABAB disinhibition, which was accompanied by an increase of gamma and a decrease of alpha oscillations in the trained hemisphere.
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG data presented in the results.

claim: Rhythmic oscillatory brain activity at rest is associated with high versus low neuronal responsiveness, or 'excitability' of a region.
source: Rhythmic oscillatory brain activity at rest is associated with high versus low neuronal responsiveness, or 'excitability' of a region (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010; Jensen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Frequency, amplitude and phase of the ongoing oscillation cycle systematically modulate responses evoked by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS).
source: Measuring these momentary fluctuations of neural activity via electro- or magnetoencephalography (EEG/MEG) over human primary motor cortex (M1), it has been demonstrated that frequency, amplitude and phase of the ongoing oscillation cycle systematically modulate responses evoked by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) (Zarkowski et al., 2006; Sauseng et al., 2009; Schaworonkow et al., 2018; Kelly et al., 2009; Mazaheri et al., 2009; Schubert et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Corticomotor excitability is significantly higher when the power (amplitude) of sensorimotor rhythms in the alpha band (8–14 Hz) are low.
source: In particular, it has been shown that corticomotor excitability is significantly higher when the power (amplitude) of sensorimotor rhythms in the alpha band (8–14 Hz, also called the 'mu'-rhythm), or beta band (15–30 Hz) are low, or when M1 is stimulated during the trough of the oscillatory cycle of these rhythms (Zaehle et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Corticomotor excitability is significantly higher when the power (amplitude) of sensorimotor rhythms in the beta band (15–30 Hz) are low.
source: In particular, it has been shown that corticomotor excitability is significantly higher when the power (amplitude) of sensorimotor rhythms in the alpha band (8–14 Hz, also called the 'mu'-rhythm), or beta band (15–30 Hz) are low, or when M1 is stimulated during the trough of the oscillatory cycle of these rhythms (Zaehle et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Corticomotor excitability is significantly higher when M1 is stimulated during the trough of the oscillatory cycle of alpha and beta rhythms.
source: In particular, it has been shown that corticomotor excitability is significantly higher when the power (amplitude) of sensorimotor rhythms in the alpha band (8–14 Hz, also called the 'mu'-rhythm), or beta band (15–30 Hz) are low, or when M1 is stimulated during the trough of the oscillatory cycle of these rhythms (Zaehle et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Stroke patients can learn to volitionally desynchronize sensorimotor rhythms with the goal of bringing the sensorimotor system into a more excitable state as a precursor for enhanced neural plasticity and accelerated recovery.
source: This concept has inspired neurofeedback interventions whereby, for example, stroke patients learn to volitionally desynchronize sensorimotor rhythms with the goal of bringing the sensorimotor system into a more excitable state as a precursor for enhanced neural plasticity and accelerated recovery (Buch et al., 2008; Caria et al., 2011; Soekadar et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on neurofeedback interventions.

claim: Primates can gain volitional control of neural activity by receiving neurofeedback via a brain-computer interface (BCI).
source: It is well known that primates (Fetz, 2013; Engelhard et al., 2013), and humans (Buch et al., 2008; Mellinger et al., 2007; Soekadar et al., 2015b; Sitaram et al., 2017; Thompson et al., 2009) can gain volitional control of neural activity by receiving neurofeedback via a brain-computer interface (BCI).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Humans can gain volitional control of neural activity by receiving neurofeedback via a brain-computer interface (BCI).
source: It is well known that primates (Fetz, 2013; Engelhard et al., 2013), and humans (Buch et al., 2008; Mellinger et al., 2007; Soekadar et al., 2015b; Sitaram et al., 2017; Thompson et al., 2009) can gain volitional control of neural activity by receiving neurofeedback via a brain-computer interface (BCI).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: MEP amplitudes increased during UP training relative to baseline measurement.
source: Across two training sessions, we found that MEP amplitudes increased during UP training (Figure 2A, orange symbols) and decreased during DOWN training (Figure 2A, blue symbols, also see Figure 2—figure supplements 2, 3 and 4) relative to the baseline measurement (BS), revealing a significant dissociation over time (neurofeedback type x block number interaction during training session 1 [F(4,115.9) = 3.87, p = 0.006], session 2 [F(4,125.0) = 3.7, p = 0.007] and EEG session [F(2,70) = 6.9, p = 0.002], F tests following mixed effects models, n = 15; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for additional analyses).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: MEP amplitudes decreased during DOWN training relative to baseline measurement.
source: Across two training sessions, we found that MEP amplitudes increased during UP training (Figure 2A, orange symbols) and decreased during DOWN training (Figure 2A, blue symbols, also see Figure 2—figure supplements 2, 3 and 4) relative to the baseline measurement (BS), revealing a significant dissociation over time (neurofeedback type x block number interaction during training session 1 [F(4,115.9) = 3.87, p = 0.006], session 2 [F(4,125.0) = 3.7, p = 0.007] and EEG session [F(2,70) = 6.9, p = 0.002], F tests following mixed effects models, n = 15; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for additional analyses).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was a significant neurofeedback type x block number interaction during training session 1 (F(4,115.9) = 3.87, p = 0.006).
source: Across two training sessions, we found that MEP amplitudes increased during UP training (Figure 2A, orange symbols) and decreased during DOWN training (Figure 2A, blue symbols, also see Figure 2—figure supplements 2, 3 and 4) relative to the baseline measurement (BS), revealing a significant dissociation over time (neurofeedback type x block number interaction during training session 1 [F(4,115.9) = 3.87, p = 0.006], session 2 [F(4,125.0) = 3.7, p = 0.007] and EEG session [F(2,70) = 6.9, p = 0.002], F tests following mixed effects models, n = 15; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for additional analyses).
evidence: This is a statistical result from mixed effects model analysis.

claim: There was a significant neurofeedback type x block number interaction during the EEG session (F(2,70) = 6.9, p = 0.002).
source: Across two training sessions, we found that MEP amplitudes increased during UP training (Figure 2A, orange symbols) and decreased during DOWN training (Figure 2A, blue symbols, also see Figure 2—figure supplements 2, 3 and 4) relative to the baseline measurement (BS), revealing a significant dissociation over time (neurofeedback type x block number interaction during training session 1 [F(4,115.9) = 3.87, p = 0.006], session 2 [F(4,125.0) = 3.7, p = 0.007] and EEG session [F(2,70) = 6.9, p = 0.002], F tests following mixed effects models, n = 15; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for additional analyses).
evidence: This is a statistical result from mixed effects model analysis.

claim: MEP amplitudes are a compound measure of excitability influenced by multiple neural elements, including background muscle activity.
source: Since MEP amplitudes are a compound measure of excitability influenced by multiple neural elements (Carson et al., 2016), including background muscle activity (Hess et al., 1986; Devanne et al., 1997), we repeated this analysis using the root mean squared (rms) background muscle activation (EMG) recorded in the 100 ms prior to each TMS pulse.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The observed modulation of MEP amplitude was not driven by changes in peripheral activity of the target muscle.
source: Importantly, this control analysis revealed no such interactions on any of the sessions, suggesting that the observed modulation was not driven by changes in peripheral activity of the target muscle, nor any of the additional three control muscles (OP, ADM, left FDI) (all p > 0.18, see Supplementary file 1 Table 2, in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by control analyses of background EMG data.

claim: The control group exhibited no systematic changes of corticomotor excitability across training.
source: This group exhibited no systematic changes of corticomotor excitability across training (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3) and mixed effects models revealed no significant neurofeedback type x block number interactions on any of the separate testing sessions in the control group (all p > 0.06, note that statistics approached significance for the second session because MEPs were randomly higher in the DOWN than in the UP condition; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1 for further details).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The experimental group exhibited on average MEP amplitudes twice as large during UP than during DOWN.
source: The differences were substantial in the experimental group, who exhibited on average MEP amplitudes twice as large during UP than during DOWN, and differed significantly from the control group where systematic differences were virtually absent (effect of 'Group' [F(1,25.6) = 13.32, p = 0.001], F tests following mixed effects, n = 28).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison between experimental and control groups.

claim: There was a significant effect of 'Group' (F(1,25.6) = 13.32, p = 0.001) when comparing experimental and control groups.
source: The differences were substantial in the experimental group, who exhibited on average MEP amplitudes twice as large during UP than during DOWN, and differed significantly from the control group where systematic differences were virtually absent (effect of 'Group' [F(1,25.6) = 13.32, p = 0.001], F tests following mixed effects, n = 28).
evidence: This is a statistical result from mixed effects model analysis.

claim: Veridical TMS neurofeedback was essential for gaining volitional control over corticomotor excitability.
source: As the control group were executing the same mental imagery strategies as the experimental group, this comparison demonstrates that vertical TMS neurofeedback was essential for gaining volitional control over corticomotor excitability.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison between experimental and control groups.

claim: Participants retained the ability to upregulate and downregulate their MEP amplitude with neurofeedback approximately 6 months following initial neurofeedback training.
source: In a follow-up investigation approximately 6 months following initial neurofeedback training, we showed for a subset of the participants (n = 11) that they had retained the ability to upregulate and downregulate their MEP amplitude with neurofeedback (Figure 3; significant effect of neurofeedback type (UP vs DOWN) in a retention block carried out with no top-up training (F(1,10)=6.64, p = 0.028).
evidence: This claim is supported by follow-up experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: There was a significant effect of neurofeedback type (UP vs DOWN) in a retention block (F(1,10)=6.64, p = 0.028).
source: In a follow-up investigation approximately 6 months following initial neurofeedback training, we showed for a subset of the participants (n = 11) that they had retained the ability to upregulate and downregulate their MEP amplitude with neurofeedback (Figure 3; significant effect of neurofeedback type (UP vs DOWN) in a retention block carried out with no top-up training (F(1,10)=6.64, p = 0.028).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the retention experiment.

claim: Measurements of resting MEP amplitude taken 5 and 10 min following the retention block indicated no after-effects.
source: Measurements of resting MEP amplitude taken 5 and 10 min following the retention block indicated no after-effects (all p > 0.2) indicating that subjects could acutely control corticomotor excitability without long-lasting after-effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements taken after the retention block.

claim: Subjects could acutely control corticomotor excitability without long-lasting after-effects.
source: Measurements of resting MEP amplitude taken 5 and 10 min following the retention block indicated no after-effects (all p > 0.2) indicating that subjects could acutely control corticomotor excitability without long-lasting after-effects.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the absence of after-effects in the measurements.

claim: MEP amplitude was significantly larger in the UP versus DOWN condition in a feedback-free block (F(1,10) = 12.32, p = 0.006).
source: Performing a feedback-free block, we found that MEP amplitude was significantly larger in the UP versus DOWN condition (F(1,10) = 12.32, p = 0.006), indicating that when participants have reached a sufficient level of training they have optimised their mental strategies and no longer require continuous feedback.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the feedback-free block experiment.

claim: When participants have reached a sufficient level of training they have optimised their mental strategies and no longer require continuous feedback.
source: Performing a feedback-free block, we found that MEP amplitude was significantly larger in the UP versus DOWN condition (F(1,10) = 12.32, p = 0.006), indicating that when participants have reached a sufficient level of training they have optimised their mental strategies and no longer require continuous feedback.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the successful performance in the feedback-free condition.

claim: The same pattern of upregulation and downregulation of MEP amplitudes was observed in the opposite hemisphere.
source: We found that the same pattern of upregulation and downregulation of MEP amplitudes was observed in the opposite hemisphere, an effect that approached significance (F(1,20) = 4.032, p = 0.07) but was much smaller than in the neurofeedback hemisphere particularly for the UP condition (UP d = 1.01 for neurofeedback hemi, d = 0.27 for opp. hemi, DOWN d = 0.40 for neurofeedback hemi, d = 0.35 for opp. hemi, Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from the opposite hemisphere shown in Figure 3.

claim: Short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI) is believed to reflect postsynaptic GABAA inhibition.
source: Finally, we investigated which excitatory/inhibitory circuits may have contributed to the changes in corticomotor excitability, using paired pulse TMS measures of three different neurophysiological processes: (i) Short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI), believed to reflect postsynaptic GABAA inhibition (Fisher et al., 2002);
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Long interval intra-cortical inhibition (LICI) is considered as a marker for postsynaptic GABAB inhibition.
source: (ii) Long interval intra-cortical inhibition (LICI), considered as a marker for postsynaptic GABAB inhibition;
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about LICI.

claim: Late-cortical disinhibition (LCD) is thought to measure presynaptic GABAB disinhibition.
source: and (iii) late-cortical disinhibition (LCD), which is thought to measure presynaptic GABAB disinhibition, and manifests as a period in which MEP amplitude returns to and typically overshoots baseline levels, in a time window following LICI (~220 ms after a suprathreshold conditioning TMS pulse; Cash et al., 2011; Cash et al., 2010; Caux-Dedeystère et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Single pulse MEPs collected during paired-pulse measurement blocks revealed significantly larger MEP amplitudes for the UP than the DOWN condition.
source: Single pulse MEPs collected during these measurement blocks (25% of all trials) revealed significantly larger MEP amplitudes for the UP than the DOWN condition, replicating the findings of the main experiment (Figure 4A; significant time point x neurofeedback type interaction: F(1,27.67) = 14.36, pFDR = 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There were no significant differences in the magnitude of SICI between the resting baseline data and the SICI MEPs collected during neurofeedback.
source: Surprisingly, there were no significant differences in the magnitude of SICI (% of single pulse MEPs) between the resting baseline data and the SICI MEPs collected during neurofeedback, nor between the UP versus DOWN states (time point x neurofeedback type interaction [F(1,28.31)= 0.08, pFDR = 0.77]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of SICI data.

claim: There were no significant differences in the magnitude of LICI between the UP versus DOWN states.
source: The same was true for LICI (time point x neurofeedback type interaction [F(1,28.90) = 0.02, pFDR = 0.88]).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of LICI data.

claim: Circuits controlling postsynaptic inhibition did not seem to be differentially modulated by the UP versus DOWN state.
source: Thus, circuits controlling postsynaptic inhibition did not seem to be differentially modulated by the UP versus DOWN state.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of significant differences in SICI and LICI.

claim: For LCD there was a significant time point x neurofeedback type interaction (F(1,28.35) = 12.09, pFDR = 0.002).
source: However, for LCD there was a significant time point x neurofeedback type interaction (F(1,28.35) = 12.09, pFDR = 0.002, Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from paired-pulse TMS analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: LCD was significantly elevated in the UP condition when compared to the baseline measurement taken immediately before neurofeedback.
source: Pairwise comparisons revealed that LCD was significantly elevated in the UP condition, when compared to the baseline measurement taken immediately before neurofeedback (Figure 4B, right panel, MeanDiff = 50.9%, df = 28.35, p < 0.001) and when compared to the equivalent data recorded in the DOWN condition (MeanDiff = 56.1%, df = 28.76, p < 0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by pairwise comparisons shown in Figure 4B.

claim: LCD was significantly elevated in the UP condition when compared to the equivalent data recorded in the DOWN condition.

evidence: This claim is supported by pairwise comparisons shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For the DOWN condition LCD did not differ significantly from baseline (p = 0.45).
source: For the DOWN condition LCD did not differ significantly from baseline (p = 0.45).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the LCD analysis.

claim: UP- versus DOWN regulating corticomotor excitability caused reduced band-limited power in the theta band.
source: Figure 5a–f (n = 14) shows that UP- versus DOWN regulating corticomotor excitability caused reduced band-limited power in the theta and alpha band (blue areas in Figure 5b–d) while gamma power was clearly increased. (red areas in Figure 5e,f).
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG data shown in Figure 5.

evidence: This claim is supported by EEG data shown in Figure 5.

claim: UP- versus DOWN regulating corticomotor excitability caused increased gamma power.

source: Wilcoxon signed rank tests revealed significantly higher power for the UP than DOWN condition in the Delta (pFDR = 0.024, d = 0.754), Low Gamma (pFDR = 0.024, d = 0.753) and High Gamma (pFDR = 0.016, d = 0.712) band and significantly lower power for UP than DOWN in the theta (pFDR = 0.003, d = 0.947), low alpha (pFDR = 0.004, d = 0.805) and high alpha band (pFDR = 0.007, d = 0.714).
evidence: This is a statistical result from EEG analysis.

claim: Only the theta rhythm showed significantly lower power for the UP than the DOWN state in the opposite hemisphere (pFDR < 0.001, d = 1.071).
source: Although the feedback was lateralised to MEPs from the right limb (left hemisphere motor hotspot), we also quantified the same neural oscillations at the corresponding location in the opposite hemisphere. Here, only the theta rhythm showed significantly lower power for the UP than the DOWN state (pFDR < 0.001, d = 1.071, see Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from EEG analysis of the opposite hemisphere.

claim: Lower amplitude oscillations in theta were predictive of larger MEP amplitudes (pFDR = 0.024).
source: Lower amplitude oscillations in theta (pFDR = 0.024, Figure 5h), low alpha (pFDR < 0.001) and high alpha (pFDR = 0.002) were predictive of larger MEP amplitudes, and higher amplitude oscillations in low gamma (pFDR = 0.020) and high gamma (pFDR = 0.020) were significant predictors of larger MEP amplitudes.
evidence: This is a statistical result from regression analysis shown in Figure 5h.

source: Lower amplitude oscillations in theta (pFDR = 0.024, Figure 5h), low alpha (pFDR < 0.001) and high alpha (pFDR = 0.002) were predictive of larger MEP amplitudes, and higher amplitude oscillations in low gamma (pFDR = 0.020) and high gamma (pFDR = 0.020) were significant predictors of larger MEP amplitudes.

claim: The low gamma: high alpha ratio was a significant predictor of MEP amplitude (pFDR = 0.016) with larger ratios predicting larger MEP amplitudes.
source: In a previous study, it was reported that a strong predictor of cortical excitability was the low gamma: high alpha ratio (Zarkowski et al., 2006). We replicated this finding, demonstrating that this ratio was a significant predictor of MEP amplitude (pFDR = 0.016) with larger ratios predicting larger MEP amplitudes.
evidence: This claim replicates a previous finding and is supported by regression analysis.

claim: A linear support vector machine (SVM) was capable of classifying the brain states with an average accuracy of 81.5% (±5.1%) using only data from the electrode closest to the hotspot.
source: Using only data from the electrode closest to the hotspot (eight rhythms plus LowGamma:HighAlpha ratio) the SVM was capable of classifying the brain states with an average accuracy of 81.5% (±5.1%) based on 10-fold cross validation which differed significantly (p = 0.001, n = 14) from a null model revealed by permutation testing (accuracy null model: 49.0% ± 13).
evidence: This is a result from machine learning classification analysis.

claim: The SVM classification accuracy differed significantly (p = 0.001, n = 14) from a null model revealed by permutation testing.
source: Using only data from the electrode closest to the hotspot (eight rhythms plus LowGamma:HighAlpha ratio) the SVM was capable of classifying the brain states with an average accuracy of 81.5% (±5.1%) based on 10-fold cross validation which differed significantly (p = 0.001, n = 14) from a null model revealed by permutation testing (accuracy null model: 49.0% ± 13).
evidence: This is a statistical result from machine learning classification analysis.

claim: Incorporating data from the same rhythms recorded at the corresponding electrode in the opposite hemisphere increased classification accuracy to 85.1% (±4.6%).
source: Additionally, incorporating data from the same rhythms recorded at the corresponding electrode in the opposite hemisphere increased this accuracy to 85.1% (±4.6%) across participants (see Supplementary file 1 Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from machine learning classification analysis.

claim: The strongest contribution to the high classification accuracy was the High Gamma rhythm in the hotspot electrode.
source: Using feature ranking based on Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE), taking the mode of the top ranked features across participants revealed that the strongest contribution to the high classification accuracy of the latter SVM was the High Gamma rhythm in the hotspot electrode, followed by High Alpha at the hotspot, then the LowGamma:HighAlpha ratio (for full ranking order see Supplementary file 1 Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from feature ranking analysis.

claim: Using a bidirectional TMS-neurofeedback approach is critical to gain volitional control over MEP amplitudes.
source: Here we aimed to uncover neural activity evoked by voluntarily facilitating or suppressing excitability within sensorimotor circuits, while keeping motor or muscle contraction-related sensory feedback constant. We show that using a bidirectional TMS-neurofeedback approach is critical to gain volitional control over MEP amplitudes, a skill that is retained for at least 6 months without further training.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results comparing experimental and control groups.

claim: The skill of volitional control over MEP amplitudes is retained for at least 6 months without further training.
source: Here we aimed to uncover neural activity evoked by voluntarily facilitating or suppressing excitability within sensorimotor circuits, while keeping motor or muscle contraction-related sensory feedback constant. We show that using a bidirectional TMS-neurofeedback approach is critical to gain volitional control over MEP amplitudes, a skill that is retained for at least 6 months without further training.
evidence: This claim is supported by the retention experiment data.

claim: Voluntary state-setting with a large dynamic range was related to variation in a paired-pulse TMS proxy measure of pre-synaptic GABAB mediated disinhibition.
source: This voluntary state-setting with a large dynamic range was related to variation in a paired-pulse TMS proxy measure of pre-synaptic GABAB mediated disinhibition, and to a prominent increase of gamma power in sensorimotor cortex for the UP state which was accompanied by a clear reduction of power in the theta, low and high alpha bands.
evidence: This claim is supported by paired-pulse TMS and EEG data.

claim: Voluntary upregulation of corticomotor excitability was accompanied by a prominent increase of gamma power in sensorimotor cortex.
source: This voluntary state-setting with a large dynamic range was related to variation in a paired-pulse TMS proxy measure of pre-synaptic GABAB mediated disinhibition, and to a prominent increase of gamma power in sensorimotor cortex for the UP state which was accompanied by a clear reduction of power in the theta, low and high alpha bands.
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG data.

claim: Voluntary upregulation of corticomotor excitability was accompanied by a clear reduction of power in the theta, low and high alpha bands.
source: This voluntary state-setting with a large dynamic range was related to variation in a paired-pulse TMS proxy measure of pre-synaptic GABAB mediated disinhibition, and to a prominent increase of gamma power in sensorimotor cortex for the UP state which was accompanied by a clear reduction of power in the theta, low and high alpha bands.
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG data.

claim: LCD is thought to represent a read-out of the presynaptic self-inhibition of GABAergic neurons which is thought to be mediated by extrasynaptic GABAB auto-receptors.
source: LCD is thought to represent a read-out of the presynaptic self-inhibition of GABAergic neurons which is thought to be mediated by extrasynaptic GABAB auto-receptors (Mott and Lewis, 1991; Sanger et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The presynaptic self-inhibition of GABAergic neurons is hypothesized to result in a net facilitatory effect.
source: This mechanism is hypothesized to result in a net facilitatory effect as observed during the UP condition in our study.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the mechanism of presynaptic self-inhibition.

claim: LCD was found to be elevated during motor imagery (MI), but this increase relative to rest was observed irrespective of whether participants imagined voluntarily activating or relaxing hand muscles.
source: Previously, LCD was found to be elevated during motor imagery (MI), but this increase relative to rest was observed irrespective of whether participants imagined voluntarily activating or relaxing hand muscles (Chong and Stinear, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The 'pulsed inhibition' theory suggests that repeated bursts of inhibitory alpha activity serve to temporarily silence gamma oscillations.
source: Our observation of reciprocal changes in the alpha and gamma band are in line with previous studies using transcranial as well as intracranial recording methods (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010). The 'pulsed inhibition' theory suggests that repeated bursts of inhibitory alpha activity serve to temporarily silence gamma oscillations (Jensen and Mazaheri, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In periods of high alpha, gamma may still burst periodically, but only at the troughs of the oscillation cycle, meaning that the gamma 'duty cycle' is short.
source: Thus, these two rhythms are seen to exhibit a reciprocal relationship, whereby when alpha is high, gamma is low. In periods of high alpha, gamma may still burst periodically, but only at the troughs of the oscillation cycle, meaning that the gamma 'duty cycle' (window for neural processing) is short, and only brief messages can be sent.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the pulsed inhibition theory.

claim: In periods of low alpha power, the gamma duty cycle is longer, and more extensive neuronal processing and inter-regional communication may occur.
source: By contrast, in periods of low alpha power, the gamma duty cycle is longer, and more extensive neuronal processing and inter-regional communication may occur.
evidence: This is an explanation based on the pulsed inhibition theory.

claim: The pharmacological removal of GABAB-mediated inhibition (by receptor blockage) in rats results in increased gamma oscillations.
source: Our finding of increased gamma activity is also consistent with previous animal literature, showing that the pharmacological removal of GABAB-mediated inhibition (by receptor blockage) in rats results in increased gamma oscillations (Leung and Shen, 2007) which have been shown to be largest in M1's layer V (Johnson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous animal research.

claim: Increased gamma oscillations following GABAB receptor blockage have been shown to be largest in M1's layer V.
source: Our finding of increased gamma activity is also consistent with previous animal literature, showing that the pharmacological removal of GABAB-mediated inhibition (by receptor blockage) in rats results in increased gamma oscillations (Leung and Shen, 2007) which have been shown to be largest in M1's layer V (Johnson et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Gamma activity is highly localised.
source: Gamma has often been considered difficult to detect using scalp electrodes because it is highly localised (Buzsaki, 2006) and may also reflect non-cortical sources when recorded with EEG (Yuval-Greenberg et al., 2008; Whitham et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Gamma may reflect non-cortical sources when recorded with EEG.
source: Gamma has often been considered difficult to detect using scalp electrodes because it is highly localised (Buzsaki, 2006) and may also reflect non-cortical sources when recorded with EEG (Yuval-Greenberg et al., 2008; Whitham et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Gamma power could be upregulated to a substantial amount which even exceeded power values observed during movement execution.
source: This suggestion is in line with previous neurofeedback studies that provided direct feedback of gamma activity, showing that gamma power could be upregulated to a substantial amount which even exceeded power values observed during movement execution (Engelhard et al., 2013; Miller et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous neurofeedback studies.

claim: Low alpha or beta power as well as high gamma power during natural fluctuations at rest are associated with larger MEP amplitudes.
source: Previous studies have taken a correlational approach to investigating the relationships between brain rhythms and corticomotor excitability. These have shown that low alpha (Sauseng et al., 2009; Zrenner et al., 2018) or beta power (Mäki and Ilmoniemi, 2010) as well as high gamma power (Zarkowski et al., 2006) during natural fluctuations at rest are associated with larger MEP amplitudes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous correlational studies.

claim: Theta showed a bilateral pattern of modulation, being higher in the DOWN than the UP state in motor areas in both hemispheres.
source: While changes in alpha and gamma were specific to the hemisphere from which feedback was provided, theta showed a bilateral pattern of modulation, being higher in the DOWN than the UP state in motor areas in both hemispheres.
evidence: This claim is supported by EEG data from both hemispheres.

claim: Mid-frontal theta activity has been linked to error monitoring.
source: While mid-frontal theta activity has been linked to error monitoring (Pezzetta et al., 2018) the role of lateralized theta activity close to the sensorimotor hotspot electrode and its symmetric counterpart is less clear.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Slower rhythms exert effects over larger distances, and are thought to be involved in long-range communication.
source: Slower rhythms exert effects over larger distances, and are thought to be involved in long-range communication (Buzsaki, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A similar pattern of upregulation and downregulation was observed in the homologous muscle in the opposite limb, albeit weaker and not statistically significant.
source: A similar pattern of upregulation and downregulation was observed in the homologous muscle in the opposite limb, albeit weaker and not statistically significant.
evidence: This claim is supported by measurements from the opposite hemisphere.

claim: Beta typically desynchronizes (together with alpha) during motor execution and motor imagery.
source: Surprisingly we did not observe differential modulation of the Beta band, which is the predominant oscillatory frequency in sensorimotor cortical regions (Baker et al., 1997; Murthy and Fetz, 1996). It typically desynchronizes (together with alpha) during motor execution and motor imagery (Ramos-Murguialday and Birbaumer, 2015; Pfurtscheller and Neuper, 1997; Pfurtscheller and Berghold, 1989; Alegre et al., 2004) and has been associated with corticomotor excitability at rest (Zarkowski et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Beta has been associated with corticomotor excitability at rest.
source: Surprisingly we did not observe differential modulation of the Beta band, which is the predominant oscillatory frequency in sensorimotor cortical regions (Baker et al., 1997; Murthy and Fetz, 1996). It typically desynchronizes (together with alpha) during motor execution and motor imagery (Ramos-Murguialday and Birbaumer, 2015; Pfurtscheller and Neuper, 1997; Pfurtscheller and Berghold, 1989; Alegre et al., 2004) and has been associated with corticomotor excitability at rest (Zarkowski et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: LCD is recruited during actual movement.
source: As it is known that LCD is recruited during actual movement (Caux-Dedeystère et al., 2015; Hammond and Vallence, 2007; Opie et al., 2015), the elevated LCD we observed in the UP condition may reflect that the neurofeedback had engaged similar mechanisms to those involved in movement execution, using only voluntary endogenous processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The elevated LCD observed in the UP condition may reflect that the neurofeedback had engaged similar mechanisms to those involved in movement execution, using only voluntary endogenous processes.
source: As it is known that LCD is recruited during actual movement (Caux-Dedeystère et al., 2015; Hammond and Vallence, 2007; Opie et al., 2015), the elevated LCD we observed in the UP condition may reflect that the neurofeedback had engaged similar mechanisms to those involved in movement execution, using only voluntary endogenous processes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the LCD findings.

claim: Pathological hyperexcitability of the non-damaged hemisphere has been hypothesized to limit recovery in some stroke patients.
source: Furthermore, as pathological hyperexcitability of the non-damaged hemisphere has been hypothesized to limit recovery in some patients (Murase et al., 2004), the TMS-neurofeedback protocol can be individually tailored either to upregulate the damaged hemisphere, down-regulate the intact hemisphere, or a combination of both, depending on the patient's specific needs.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The TMS-neurofeedback protocol can be individually tailored either to upregulate the damaged hemisphere, down-regulate the intact hemisphere, or a combination of both, depending on the patient's specific needs.
source: Furthermore, as pathological hyperexcitability of the non-damaged hemisphere has been hypothesized to limit recovery in some patients (Murase et al., 2004), the TMS-neurofeedback protocol can be individually tailored either to upregulate the damaged hemisphere, down-regulate the intact hemisphere, or a combination of both, depending on the patient's specific needs.
evidence: This is a proposed application of the TMS-neurofeedback protocol.

claim: Fifteen healthy volunteers participated in the experimental group.
source: Fifteen healthy volunteers (age 23 ± 3.14 s.d, seven female) participated in the experimental group.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: An additional thirteen participants formed a control group.
source: An additional thirteen participants (age 25 ± 3.06 s.d, three female) formed a control group.
evidence: This is a description of the control group participants.

claim: All participants were right handed according to the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory.
source: All participants were right handed according to the Edinburgh Handedness Inventory (Oldfield, 1971), and gave informed consent to procedures.
evidence: This is a description of participant characteristics.

claim: The experiments were approved by the Kantonale Ethikkommission Zürich (KEK-ZH-Nr. 2014–0242).
source: The experiments were approved by the Kantonale Ethikkommission Zürich (KEK-ZH-Nr. 2014–0242), and were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: The experiments were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: The experiments were approved by the Kantonale Ethikkommission Zürich (KEK-ZH-Nr. 2014–0242), and were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical compliance.

claim: During UP training MEP amplitudes were increasingly elevated compared to baseline reaching an increase of 83.8% (±31.1 SEM) during the final block of EEG session (block 10).
source: During the UP training sessions, MEP amplitudes were increasingly elevated compared to baseline reaching an increase of 83.8% (±31.1 SEM) during the final block of EEG session (block 10).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: For the UP training, elevations in MEP amplitude were significantly different from 0 by the end of 60 neurofeedback trials (block 2).
source: These elevations in MEP amplitude were significantly different from 0 (indicating no change) by the end of 60 neurofeedback trials (block 2), and remained significantly elevated throughout all the remaining blocks (Wilcoxon Signed Rank test, two tailed, all p < 0.03, p values FDR corrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: For the DOWN training MEP amplitudes were reduced by 30.6% (±8.7 SEM) at the end of the final EEG session (block 10).
source: For the DOWN training MEP amplitudes changed less rapidly than in the UP sessions but were reduced by 30.6% (±8.7 SEM) at the end of the final EEG session (block 10).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The decreases in MEP amplitude during DOWN training were significantly different from 0 after 210 neurofeedback trials (block 7).
source: The decreases in MEP amplitude were significantly different from 0 after 210 neurofeedback trials (block 7, Wilcoxon Signed Rank test, two tailed, p = 0.006) and in the final block (10), after 300 training trials (p = 0.016, all p values FDR corrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the experimental data.

claim: For the control group, there were no significant deviations from 0 (no change) in any of the 10 blocks of UP training or DOWN training.
source: For the control group shown in panel (B), there were no significant deviations from 0 (no change) in any of the 10 blocks of UP training or DOWN training (Wilcoxon Signed Rank tests, two tailed, all p > 0.11, p values FDR corrected for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the control group data.
